headline_insight: For roughly six in seven VisionFund clients, VisionFund is their first-ever insurance provider — 86.0% of women and 84.8% of men had no access before — and around half of all clients (52.0% of women, 50.9% of men) say obtaining comparable cover elsewhere would be "very difficult."
paragraphs: VisionFund is functioning, for the overwhelming majority of its clients, as the point of first entry into formal insurance. Among 1,518 female and 586 male respondents, 86.0% of women and 84.8% of men reported having had no access to insurance before VisionFund — a gap of just 1.2 percentage points that is not statistically significant (adjusted p = 0.7). The same pattern holds for clients in households that include a person with a disability: 84.3% of the 477 PWD-household respondents were first-time users, compared with 86.1% of the 1,621 non-PWD households, again a difference of under two percentage points and not significant. Both subgroup samples are adequately powered (n_ok = true), so the absence of a gap here should be read as a genuine finding rather than an artefact of small numbers.

The counterfactual data reinforces how thin the alternatives are. Asked how easy it would be to obtain similar cover elsewhere, 52.0% of women and 50.9% of men answered "very difficult," with a further 17.8% and 18.9% respectively saying "slightly difficult" — meaning close to seven in ten clients of either gender see no straightforward substitute. Only 4.6% of women and 5.5% of men described alternative access as "very easy." PWD households mirror this almost exactly (53.0% "very difficult" versus 51.3% for non-PWD households). One difference worth noting, even though it does not reach significance after adjustment, is that women were somewhat more likely than men to answer "I don't know" (13.1% versus 9.9%, pt_diff 3.2, adjusted p = 0.2) — a directional signal that women may have less visibility into the wider insurance market rather than a demonstrated inequality.

Two limitations should be stated plainly. No qualitative material was returned for this section of the survey, so no client voice can be quoted here in support of the quantitative pattern; the interpretation above rests on the closed-response data alone, and future rounds should pair these items with open-ended probes on why alternatives are perceived as difficult. Likewise, no external benchmark data was supplied for either first-time access or perceived ease of alternative access, so these figures cannot be positioned against national or peer-institution norms — any such comparison would have to be commissioned separately. Broader development-sector framing on the insurance protection gap is general context, not a finding of this survey.

For programming, the implication is twofold. First, because uptake is overwhelmingly first-time across every subgroup measured, product design and client education cannot assume prior insurance literacy — onboarding, claims explanation, and renewal communication must be built for a first-time user by default, not as a remedial add-on. Second, the near-identical results for women, men, and PWD households mean the binding constraint at this stage is market absence rather than differential exclusion within VisionFund's reach; the equity question shifts from "who gets in" to "who is reached in the first place" and to whether experience after enrolment remains equally positive. The slightly elevated "I don't know" rate among women is the one thread worth monitoring, and it argues for testing whether women receive the same quality of comparative information about their options as men do.
